After asking a question about what minerals you can put in a fish tank. I came to some useful recources about what minerals can be used. http://www.myaquariumclub.com/safe-and-unsafe-aquarium-rocks-533.html

On the whole, Quartz is a good crystal to use. Its silica based and is unreactive at our atmospheric temperature. It also doesn't disolve in water at all and contains nothing but silica which is fine to go in a tank. Quartz, comes in a variety of colours (eg. purple or otherwise know as amethyst.) This also means that quartz based rocks are ideal to put in your tank. Sand is made up of quartz, which is why it scratches glass and acrylic as its a hard mineral. Metamorphosed sandstone would also be good to use in the tank as the grains have crystalised so it won't crumble and add to the sediment in your tank, however it does contain calcite so will increase your ph.

Rocks like granite which contain quartz can also be used, however its worth mentioning that these contain feldspar which reacts aggressively with acid and breaks down into clays. Rain water is enough to break feldspar down as it is a very reactive substance. Rainwater on average has a PH of 5.6 (roughly).

Any minerals which contain metals should not be used. So malchalite, zinc copper ect. are not good to use at all. This rules out minerals like Galena (which contains lead) Chromite (chromium) Zincite and Barite and anything else along those lines. If you see a rock that looks pretty, but you aren't sure what it is...then look it up! http://gwydir.demon.co.uk/jo/minerals/metals.htm (link to some metals)

Slate is great for fish tanks. Its made up of broken down feldspar aka clay so it can't react with anything! Its an impermeable rock and it breaks easily and can be broken into attractive chunks. Please note: Slate is good because it has metamorphosed and become crystaline meaning the crystals interlock. However, shale although looks similar is not good as its only compacted sediment and crumbles easily which can add unwanted sediment to your tank.

This also means that anything which comes from a mudstone like shale is good for your tank. Slate is the most readily availiable however rocks which are made of the same stuff which have been metamorphosed further but look more attractive than slate are:

Spotted rock: https://wwwf.imperial.ac.uk/earthscienceandengineering/rocklibrary/shared/hs_J_0.jpg

Hornfels: http://flexiblelearning.auckland.ac.nz/rocks_minerals/rocks/images/hornfels1.jpg (this glitters)

Schist:http://flexiblelearning.auckland.ac.nz/rocks_minerals/rocks/images/schist3.jpg

Gniess: http://geology.com/rocks/pictures/gneiss.jpg

All these are good to use!

Limestones and other fossil based rocks should be avoided. Limestones contain calcite from dead sea creatures. These will raise your Ph. Fossils can also look pretty, however, some fossils form from Iron pyrite which should be avoided. It looks like this: http://geology.com/minerals/photos/pyrite-ammonite-istock.jpg Other fossils can for through calcification which means they involve calcite! Which will disolve and increase your ph. Quartz fossils are okay to use, but are really rare. Pertrifed trees can be used too.

Salt rocks should be avoided as they will disolve in water.

Rocks formed through a volcanic explosion eg: basalt, pumice, dolorite can be used in your tank as these are either silicic or basaltic rocks with very little mineral diversity in them as they have cooled down ultrea fast. Obsidian can be used too and onyx.

Hope people find this useful, I'm going to go turn my tank into a quartz crystal garden! :D
